text: every closed C^r 1-form on a simply connected manifold is the differential of a C^r function, so H¹_dR vanishes (Lee, *Introduction to Smooth Manifolds*, Ch. 11).

name: Semisimple linear Lie algebras contain the Jordan parts of their elements
text: a semisimple Lie subalgebra of 𝔤𝔩(V) over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero contains the semisimple and nilpotent parts of each element, so faithful representations preserve the abstract Jordan decomposition (Humphreys, *Introduction to Lie Algebras*, §6.4).

name: The dual Jacobi–Trudi identity
text: s_μ = det(e_{μ′ᵢ − i + j}) in the elementary symmetric polynomials over any commutative ring, the half left open when the Jacobi–Trudi identity was announced (Macdonald, *Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials*, I (3.5)).

name: Symplectic transvections generate the symplectic group
text: over every field, in any characteristic, the symplectic transvections generate Sp_{2m}(K) (Artin, *Geometric Algebra*, Ch. III).

name: Topological generators of tori
text: every compact connected abelian Lie group has an element generating a dense subgroup, and such generators form a dense set (Bröcker–tom Dieck, *Representations of Compact Lie Groups*, I.4.14).

name: Lakshmibai–Seshadri paths
text: Littelmann's encoding of the LS paths of shape λ by decreasing chains of Weyl-group cosets and rational times satisfying the a-chain condition, finitely many for each λ (Littelmann, *Invent. Math.* 116 (1994)).

name: Killing vector fields
text: vector fields X with L_X g = 0, characterised by skew-adjointness of ∇X, with ∇²X = R(·, X)· and the restriction of X to any geodesic a Jacobi field (Petersen, *Riemannian Geometry*, Ch. 8).

name: Stable distributions
text: the probability laws on ℝ with the stable characteristic function of index α ∈ (0, 2], skewness |β| ≤ 1, scale and location, in Nolan's S₀ parametrisation (Nolan, *Univariate Stable Distributions*, Ch. 1).

name: Borel–Moore homology
text: the homology of locally finite singular chains with local coefficients, agreeing with ordinary homology on compact spaces (Bredon, *Sheaf Theory*, Ch. V).

name: The affine Weyl group
text: the group generated by the affine reflections s_{α,k} of a root pairing, whose elements are exactly the affine maps with linear part in W and translation in the coroot lattice, W_aff = Q^∨ ⋊ W (Humphreys, *Reflection Groups and Coxeter Groups*, §4.2).

name: The group Spinᶜ
text: Spinᶜ(Q) = (Spin(Q) × U(1))/{±1}, with its determinant map to U(1) and its map to SO(Q), the kernel of their product being of order two (Lawson–Michelsohn, *Spin Geometry*, App. D).

name: The fundamental group of a graph of groups
text: Serre's π₁(𝔸, T): the free product of the vertex groups and the free group on the edges, modulo the edge relations and the edges of T (Serre, *Trees*, I §5.1).

name: Hirzebruch's multiplicative sequences
text: the polynomials K_k in the elementary symmetric functions with Σ K_k = ∏ Q(xᵢ) for a power series Q, multiplicative on disjoint unions of roots (Hirzebruch, *Topological Methods in Algebraic Geometry*, §1).

name: The Turing jump
text: Z′ = {e : the e-th Z-computable program halts on input e}, with Z <_T Z′ and every Z-c.e. set one-one reducible to Z′ (Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, III.2).

name: The lemniscate constant
text: ϖ = 2∫₀¹ dt/√(1 − t⁴), the half-length of the lemniscate, with the closed form ϖ = Γ(1/4)²/(2√(2π)) (Borwein–Borwein, *Pi and the AGM*, Ch. 1).
Correctly stated: every finite abelian extension of ℚ embeds in some ℚ(ζₙ), n ≠ 0 (Washington, Introduction to Cyclotomic Fields, Thm 14.1; Wikipedia); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: π_{n+1}(Γ K, 0) ≃ H_{n+1}(K) for a nonnegatively graded chain complex of R-modules, natural in chain maps (Goerss–Jardine, Simplicial Homotopy Theory, Cor. III.2.7); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: π₀(Γ K) ≃ H₀(K) (Goerss–Jardine III.2.7); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: with [1], …, [n] units, the unique idempotent of augmentation 1 killed on both sides by every eᵢ, the Jones–Wenzl projection (Wenzl 1987; Kauffman–Lins, Temperley–Lieb Recoupling Theory, Ch. 3); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: for p + q ≥ 2 the image of Spin(p, q) → SO(p, q) is the identity component SO₀(p, q) (Lawson–Michelsohn, Spin Geometry, I §2; Wikipedia, Spin group, indefinite signature); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: over an algebraically closed field, G / R_u(G) is a torus for a reduced connected solvable affine group of finite type (Borel, Linear Algebraic Groups, Thm 10.6(1); Humphreys 19.3(a)); the docstring claims no splitting G = T ⋉ G_u; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: in the Black–Scholes market with physical drift μ, callValue at S_u equals e^{−r(T−u)} E_Q[(S_T − K)⁺ | ℱ_u] Q-a.s. under the Girsanov-tilted risk-neutral measure (Shreve, Stochastic Calculus for Finance II, §§5.2.4–5.2.5); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: on a closed manifold, PSC metrics joined by a path of PSC metrics continuous in the chart C² topology are concordant (Gromov–Lawson, Ann. of Math. 111 (1980), Lemma 3); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: Newton above Hodge for a matrix with a Smith normal form over a ring with a nonnegative valuation, finite v(det A) (Kedlaya, A little p-adic numerical analysis, §3 Thm 16); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: the slope-data form of Newton above Hodge (Kedlaya, A little p-adic numerical analysis, §3 Thm 16); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: the Newton polygon of det(1 − XA) at n is Σ v(sᵢ), the Hodge endpoint (Kedlaya, §3 Thm 16); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: κ(G) ≤ λ(G) for every simple graph, Whitney's inequality (Diestel, Graph Theory, Prop. 1.4.2; Whitney 1932); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: PGL(2, K) is sharply 3-transitive on P¹(K), normalised at (0, 1, ∞) (Wikipedia, Projective linear group; Ahlfors, Complex Analysis, Ch. 3 §3.3 for K = ℂ); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: the three roots of (X + 16)³ − jX are the twelfth powers of the level-two Siegel functions, Weber's identities (𝔣²⁴ − 16)³ = j𝔣²⁴, (𝔣ᵢ²⁴ + 16)³ = j𝔣ᵢ²⁴ in Siegel-function form (Wikipedia, Weber modular function; Cox, Primes of the Form x² + ny², §12); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: the nuclear operators E → F with the nuclear norm, the quotient of E* ⊗̂π F by the kernel of the canonical map (Ryan, Introduction to Tensor Products of Banach Spaces, Ch. 2); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: B ⊆ A whose leading terms generate the initial algebra of A (Robbiano–Sweedler 1990; Sturmfels, Gröbner Bases and Convex Polytopes, Ch. 11); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: the group presented on simple classes by [S][T] = [U] whenever Hom(U, S ⊗ T) ≠ 0, the universal grading group (EGNO, Tensor Categories, §4.14); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: some resolvent is a compact operator, equivalently every one (Kato, Perturbation Theory for Linear Operators, III §6.8; Reed–Simon IV, XIII.14); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: chart-locally induced by an adic morphism of Huber pairs (Huber, Math. Z. 217 (1994), §3), with the analytic-points characterisation Prop. 3.2(ii); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: H^k_c(E) = 0 for k ≠ dim E on a finite-dimensional real normed space, the vanishing half of the Poincaré lemma for compact supports (Bott–Tu, §4; Lee, Thm 17.28); the top degree is a separate statement, as the docstring says; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: Grothendieck's inequality for bounded bilinear forms on C(K) × C(L) with the constant 16, not sharp, as the docstring says (Albiac–Kalton, Topics in Banach Space Theory, 8.1.3); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: Menger's theorem, internally vertex-disjoint paths, for multigraphs with finitely many vertices (Menger 1927; Schrijver, Combinatorial Optimization, §9.1); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: the undirected max-flow/min-cut theorem for nonnegative edge capacities on a multigraph (Ford–Fulkerson, Flows in Networks, Ch. I); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: the Littlewood–Richardson rule with c^ν_{λμ} the number of Littlewood–Richardson tableaux of shape ν/λ and content μ (Fulton, Young Tableaux, §5.1); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: the Littlewood–Richardson rule for rational Weyl modules of GLₙ(ℂ) indexed by arbitrary dominant weights, via determinant twists (Fulton–Harris, Lecture 6 and §15.5); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.
Correctly stated: flasque sheaves of modules have Extⁿ⁺¹(R_U, F) = 0, so are acyclic (Hartshorne, Prop. III.2.5); compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: the stable category of Gorenstein-projective objects of an abelian category embeds fully faithfully into D^b(C)/Perf(C) (X.-W. Chen, Math. Nachr. 284 (2011), Thm 2.1); the docstring claims only the fully faithful half of Buchweitz; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

Correctly stated: the lattice glued from a row of the rootful rank-24 table along its glue code (Conway–Sloane, SPLAG, Ch. 16 §1, Table 16.1); unimodularity is proved for 19 rows and labelled so; compared in Voyager's full-statement test.

name: The Kronecker–Weber theorem
text: every finite abelian extension of ℚ embeds in a cyclotomic field ℚ(ζₙ) (Washington, *Introduction to Cyclotomic Fields*, Thm 14.1).

name: Homotopy groups under Dold–Kan
text: for a nonnegatively graded chain complex K of R-modules, the homotopy groups of the simplicial module Γ(K) are the homology groups of K, π₀ included, naturally in chain maps (Goerss–Jardine, *Simplicial Homotopy Theory*, III.2.7).

name: Jones–Wenzl projections
text: when the quantum integers [1], …, [n] are invertible, the Temperley–Lieb algebra TLₙ(δ) has exactly one idempotent of augmentation 1 killed on both sides by every generator eᵢ, given by Wenzl's recursion (Wenzl, *C. R. Math. Rep. Acad. Sci. Canada* 9 (1987)).

name: The image of Spin(p, q) is SO₀(p, q)
text: for p + q ≥ 2 the image of Spin(p, q) → SO(p, q) is the identity component SO₀(p, q), the kernel of the spinor norm, so with the kernel {±1} announced earlier Spin(p, q) double covers SO₀(p, q) (Lawson–Michelsohn, *Spin Geometry*, I §2).

name: The unipotent part of a connected solvable group
text: over an algebraically closed field, in every characteristic, the unipotent points of a connected solvable linear algebraic group are exactly the points of its unipotent radical, and the quotient by it is a torus (Borel, *Linear Algebraic Groups*, Thm 10.6(1)).

name: The Black–Scholes formula as a conditional risk-neutral price
text: in the Black–Scholes market with physical drift μ, the call and put prices at the spot S_u are the discounted conditional expected payoffs e^{−r(T−u)} E_Q[· | ℱ_u] under the Girsanov risk-neutral measure Q, extending the static formula of TauCeti#18827 (Shreve, *Stochastic Calculus for Finance II*, §5.2.4).

name: Isotopic metrics of positive scalar curvature are concordant
text: on a closed manifold M, PSC metrics joined by a C²-continuous path of PSC metrics are concordant: some PSC metric on M × ℝ equals g₀ + dt² for t ≤ 0 and g₁ + dt² for t ≥ 1 (Gromov–Lawson, *Ann. of Math.* 111 (1980), Lemma 3).

name: Newton above Hodge
text: for a matrix over a ring with a nonnegative valuation, such as a lattice endomorphism over a DVR, the Hodge polygon of its invariant factors lies on or below the Newton polygon of det(1 − XA), with the same endpoint (Kedlaya, *A little p-adic numerical analysis*, Thm 16).

name: Whitney's inequality
text: for a simple graph, κ(G) ≤ λ(G) ≤ δ(G): the vertex connectivity is at most the edge connectivity, which is at most the minimum degree once the graph is finite with at least two vertices (Diestel, *Graph Theory*, Prop. 1.4.2).

name: Sharp triple transitivity of Möbius transformations
text: over any field K exactly one element of PGL(2, K) carries 0, 1, ∞ to three given distinct points of the projective line, and over an algebraically closed K exactly one element of PSL(2, K) (Ahlfors, *Complex Analysis*, Ch. 3 §3.3).

name: Weber's cubic
text: the twelfth powers of the level-two Siegel functions g_{(0,1/2)}, g_{(1/2,0)}, g_{(1/2,1/2)} are the three roots of (X + 16)³ = jX, Weber's identities (𝔣²⁴ − 16)³ = j𝔣²⁴ and (𝔣ᵢ²⁴ + 16)³ = j𝔣ᵢ²⁴ in Siegel-function form (Cox, *Primes of the Form x² + ny²*, §12).

name: Nuclear operators
text: for Banach spaces E, F, the image of E* ⊗̂π F → L(E, F), a Banach space under the nuclear norm ν inherited from the projective tensor product, with ν(A∘T∘B) ≤ ‖A‖ ν(T) ‖B‖; also being formalised in mathlib4#42197 (Ryan, *Introduction to Tensor Products of Banach Spaces*, Ch. 2).

name: SAGBI bases
text: for a monomial order, the initial algebra of a subalgebra A ⊆ k[x₁, …, xₙ] is generated by the leading terms of A, and a SAGBI basis of A is a subset whose leading terms generate the initial algebra (Sturmfels, *Gröbner Bases and Convex Polytopes*, Ch. 11).

name: The universal grading group
text: the group U(C) presented on the simple objects of a tensor category C by [S][T] = [U] whenever U occurs in S ⊗ T, through which every group grading of C factors (EGNO, *Tensor Categories*, §4.14).

name: Operators with compact resolvent
text: an unbounded operator A has compact resolvent when some (λ − A)⁻¹ is a compact operator, hence all are; for self-adjoint D the bounded inverse (1 + D²)⁻¹ = R(i)*R(i) is then a positive compact operator (Kato, *Perturbation Theory for Linear Operators*, III §6.8).

name: Adic morphisms of adic spaces
text: morphisms chart-locally induced by adic homomorphisms of Huber pairs; a morphism of adic spaces is adic exactly when it sends analytic points to analytic points (Huber, *Math. Z.* 217 (1994), §3, Prop. 3.2).

name: Von Neumann's density theorem
text: an operator in the double commutant of a unital ⋆-subalgebra of the bounded operators on a Hilbert space is a strong-operator limit of elements of the subalgebra (Kadison–Ringrose, *Fundamentals of the Theory of Operator Algebras*, Thm 5.3.1).

name: The Perron–Frobenius theorem
text: now in full: an irreducible nonnegative real matrix has a positive eigenvector whose eigenvalue is positive, simple and equal to the spectral radius, and every nonnegative eigenvector is a multiple of it (Seneta, *Non-negative Matrices and Markov Chains*, Thm 1.5).

name: The Kronecker–Weber theorem, with the conductor
text: the least n with a given finite abelian extension of ℚ inside ℚ(ζₙ) is the finite part of its conductor, sharpening TauCeti#24374 (Washington, *Introduction to Cyclotomic Fields*, Ch. 3).

name: The Harish-Chandra isomorphism
text: for a split semisimple Lie algebra over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, the Harish-Chandra projection is an algebra isomorphism from the centre of U(𝔤) onto the dot-action invariants S(𝔥)^{W·}; injective here, onto in TauCeti#24546 (Humphreys, *Introduction to Lie Algebras and Representation Theory*, §23.3).

name: The structure theorem for Iwasawa modules
text: every finitely generated module over O⟦X⟧, O a complete discrete valuation ring, is pseudo-isomorphic to O⟦X⟧ʳ ⊕ ⨁ᵢ O⟦X⟧/(ϖ^{mᵢ}) ⊕ ⨁ⱼ O⟦X⟧/(Fⱼ^{nⱼ}) with the Fⱼ irreducible distinguished polynomials (Washington, *Introduction to Cyclotomic Fields*, Thm 13.12).

name: The Bochner formula
text: for a smooth function f on a Riemannian manifold, Δ|∇f|² = 2|Hess f|² + 2⟨∇f, ∇Δf⟩ + 2 Ric(∇f, ∇f) (Petersen, *Riemannian Geometry*, Ch. 9).

name: The étale fundamental group of a field is its absolute Galois group
text: for a separable closure Ω of K, the group Gal(Ω/K), acting on geometric fibres at Spec Ω → Spec K, is the fundamental group of the Galois category of finite étale K-schemes (SGA 1, Exp. V, Prop. 8.1).

name: Galois descent for modules
text: for a finite group G acting freely on a ring B with invariants A, B ⊗_A N^G ≅ N for every B-module N with semilinear G-action, and M ≅ (B ⊗_A M)^G for every A-module M (Chase–Harrison–Rosenberg 1965).

name: Deligne's theorem on integral modular forms
text: a polynomial in the coefficients a₁, …, a₆ of the universal Weierstrass equation is an integral modular form of weight k exactly when it is weighted homogeneous of weight k and lies in ℤ[c₄, c₆, Δ] (Deligne, *Courbes elliptiques: formulaire*, 1975).

name: The Euler characteristic of the Khovanov complex is the Jones polynomial
text: for an oriented link diagram, the graded Euler characteristic of the cohomology of its Khovanov bracket is, up to the normalising shifts, (q + q⁻¹) times the Jones polynomial (Khovanov, *Duke Math. J.* 101 (2000)).

name: The Kechris–Solecki–Todorcevic G₀ dichotomy
text: a graph on a Polish space with analytic edge relation either has a Borel colouring with countably many colours or admits a continuous homomorphism from G₀, and never both (Kechris–Solecki–Todorcevic, *Adv. Math.* 141 (1999)).

name: A low simple set
text: there is a computably enumerable set that is simple and low, so its Turing degree lies strictly between the computable degree and the halting degree (Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Thm VII.1.1).

name: Uniform convexity of Lᵖ
text: now for all 1 < p < ∞: Lᵖ(μ; E) is uniformly convex whenever E is, hence reflexive when E is complete, extending the range 2 ≤ p of TauCeti#20699 (Day, *Bull. Amer. Math. Soc.* 47 (1941)).

name: The Fourier inversion theorem for characteristic functions
text: a finite measure on a finite-dimensional inner product space whose characteristic function is integrable is absolutely continuous, with density the inverse Fourier transform of the characteristic function (Feller, *An Introduction to Probability Theory* II, XV.3).

name: Schauder's theorem
text: a bounded operator from a normed space into a Banach space over ℝ or ℂ is compact if and only if its adjoint is compact (Conway, *A Course in Functional Analysis*, VI.3.4).

name: The affine Weyl group acts simply transitively on alcoves
text: for a point x on no affine root hyperplane, exactly one element of the affine Weyl group carries the fundamental alcove onto the alcove of x (Humphreys, *Reflection Groups and Coxeter Groups*, §4.5).

name: Alexander's trick
text: a homeomorphism of the closed unit ball of a real normed space fixing the unit sphere is isotopic to the identity through homeomorphisms fixing the sphere (Farb–Margalit, *A Primer on Mapping Class Groups*, Lemma 2.1).

name: The elementary renewal theorem
text: for a renewal process with i.i.d. nonnegative increments not almost surely zero, the expected number of renewals by time t satisfies m(t)/t → 1/𝔼T, with limit 0 when the mean is infinite (Feller, *An Introduction to Probability Theory* II, XI.1).

name: Ocneanu's trace
text: for every parameter z there is exactly one Markov trace with parameter z on the infinite type-A Hecke algebra over a commutative ring, the trace behind Jones's construction of the HOMFLY polynomial (Jones, *Ann. of Math.* 126 (1987), Thm 5.1).

name: Chevalley's theorem on coinvariants
text: for a finite group generated by pseudoreflections, of order invertible in the field, Sym(V*) is a free module over the invariants, and for a faithful action the coinvariant algebra has dimension |G| (Humphreys, *Reflection Groups and Coxeter Groups*, §3.6).

name: The Singer–Wermer theorem
text: a bounded derivation of a commutative complex Banach algebra, unital or not, takes its values in the Jacobson radical (Singer–Wermer 1955; Dales, *Banach Algebras and Automatic Continuity*, Thm 2.7.20).

name: Capelli's theorem
text: over any field, Xⁿ − a is irreducible exactly when a is not a p-th power for any prime p dividing n and, when 4 ∣ n, a is not of the form −4b⁴; Mathlib had the odd-degree case (Lang, *Algebra*, VI Thm 9.1).

name: The Stieltjes inversion formula
text: a finite measure μ on ℝ is recovered from its Stieltjes transform m(z) = ∫ (x − z)⁻¹ dμ(x): as η → 0⁺, π⁻¹ ∫ₐᵇ Im m(x + iη) dx → μ(a, b) + ½ μ{a} + ½ μ{b} (Anderson–Guionnet–Zeitouni, *An Introduction to Random Matrices*, Thm 2.4.3).

name: Grothendieck's Galois theory of finite étale covers
text: now in full: over any connected scheme the finite étale schemes form a Galois category, with the geometric fibre at any geometric point as a fibre functor; TauCeti#23181 had affine bases (SGA 1, Exp. V, §7).

name: The free central limit theorem
text: for freely independent centred elements with uniformly bounded moments and average variance tending to σ², the moments of N^{−1/2}(a₁ + ⋯ + a_N) converge to those of the semicircle law of variance σ² (Nica–Speicher, *Lectures on the Combinatorics of Free Probability*, Thm 8.10).

name: The model existence theorem
text: a countable member of a consistency property for L_{ω₁ω} over a countable language has a countable model in which every element is named by a Henkin constant (Keisler, *Model Theory for Infinitary Logic*; Marker, *Lectures on Infinitary Model Theory*, §4.1).

name: Cohen–Macaulay rings are universally catenary
text: a Noetherian ring whose localisations at all primes are Cohen–Macaulay is universally catenary (Matsumura, *Commutative Ring Theory*, Thm 17.9).

name: Any two fibre functors of a Galois category are isomorphic
text: every natural transformation between fibre functors of a Galois category is an isomorphism, and between any two fibre functors there is one (SGA 1, Exp. V, §5).

name: The Poincaré lemma for compactly supported cohomology
text: now in full: for an n-dimensional real vector space E, H^k_c(E) vanishes for k ≠ n and integration against an orientation is an isomorphism H^n_c(E) ≅ ℝ (Bott–Tu, *Differential Forms in Algebraic Topology*, Cor. 4.7).

name: Turing degrees form an upper semilattice
text: the Turing join f ⊕ g is reducible to h exactly when both f and g are, so any two Turing degrees have a least upper bound; Mathlib has the partial order (Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, I.4).

name: Computably inseparable sets exist
text: the sets {e : φₑ(e) = 0} and {e : φₑ(e) = 1} are disjoint computably enumerable sets that no computable set separates (Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, I.3).

name: Theta series of even unimodular lattices are polynomials in E₄ and Δ
text: the theta series of an even unimodular lattice of rank 2k is a unique rational linear combination of the products E₄ᵃ Δᵇ with 4a + 12b = k (Serre, *A Course in Arithmetic*, VII §6).

name: Witt's example: the theta series does not determine the lattice
text: the even unimodular lattices E₈ ⊕ E₈ and D₁₆⁺ have the same theta series E₄² but are not isometric (Conway–Sloane, *Sphere Packings, Lattices and Groups*, Ch. 4).

name: Mertens' second theorem for number fields
text: for a number field K, the sum of 1/N𝔭 over the nonzero prime ideals of norm at most x is log log x + B_K + O(1/log x) (Rosen, *J. Ramanujan Math. Soc.* 14 (1999)).

name: Koteljanskii's inequality
text: for a positive semidefinite matrix A and index sets S, T, det A[S ∪ T] · det A[S ∩ T] ≤ det A[S] · det A[T], which contains the Hadamard–Fischer inequality (Horn–Johnson, *Matrix Analysis*, §7.8).

name: Roby's theorem on divided powers
text: for a free module M over a commutative ring, γ_d(m) ↦ m^{⊗d} is an isomorphism from the degree-d part of the divided power algebra Γ(M) onto the symmetric tensors in M^{⊗d} (Roby, *Ann. Sci. ENS* 80 (1963), Thm IV.2).

name: Pratelli's theorem
text: for an atomless source measure and a continuous cost on standard Borel spaces, the Monge infimum over transport maps equals the Kantorovich infimum over couplings, whether finite or not (Pratelli, *Ann. Inst. H. Poincaré Probab. Statist.* 43 (2007), Thm B).

name: Mal'cev's theorem
text: a finitely generated residually finite group is Hopfian: every surjective endomorphism is injective (Robinson, *A Course in the Theory of Groups*, 6.1.12).

name: Narayana numbers count noncrossing partitions by blocks
text: the noncrossing partitions of an n-element linearly ordered set into k blocks number (1/n)·C(n, k)·C(n, k − 1) (Kreweras, *Discrete Math.* 1 (1972)).

name: Quaternionic differentiability is rigid
text: a function ℍ → ℍ whose left difference quotients converge at every point of a connected open set is of the form q ↦ a + q·b there, and conversely (Sudbery, *Math. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc.* 85 (1979), Thm 1).

name: Geometrically reduced extensions are separably generated
text: a finitely generated field extension that is geometrically reduced has a transcendence basis over which it is separable algebraic, the converse of Mac Lane's criterion left open in Mathlib (Stacks 030W).

name: The Hilbert class field
text: the ray class field K_𝔪 of a modulus 𝔪, with Cl_𝔪(K) ≅ Gal(K_𝔪/K) by the Artin map; the Hilbert class field H is the case 𝔪 = 1, with Cl(K) ≅ Gal(H/K) and [H : K] = h_K (Neukirch, *Algebraic Number Theory*, VI.6).

name: Algebraic spaces
text: a presheaf on schemes that is an fppf sheaf, has representable diagonal, and admits a surjective étale atlas by a scheme (Stacks 025Y).

name: Ample line bundles
text: a line bundle class on a quasi-compact scheme is ample when the affine nonvanishing loci of sections of its positive powers cover; the structure sheaf is ample exactly when the scheme is quasi-affine (Stacks 01PS).

name: Integral perfectoid rings
text: a ring that is π-adically complete for some π with πᵖ dividing p, whose Frobenius is surjective modulo p, and whose Fontaine map θ has principal kernel (Bhatt–Morrow–Scholze, *Integral p-adic Hodge theory*, Def. 3.5).

name: The full crossed product
text: the C*-algebra A ⋊_α G of a C*-dynamical system, the completion of the twisted convolution algebra C_c(G, A) in the universal norm (Williams, *Crossed Products of C*-Algebras*, Ch. 2).

name: Borel reducibility and smooth equivalence relations
text: E ≤_B F when a Borel map f satisfies E(x, y) ↔ F(f x, f y); E is smooth when it reduces to equality on Cantor space, and the eventual-equality relation E₀ is not smooth (Gao, *Invariant Descriptive Set Theory*, Ch. 5).

name: The symplectization of a contact form
text: the one-form eᵗα on ℝ × M, whose exterior derivative is nondegenerate exactly when α is a contact form (Geiges, *An Introduction to Contact Topology*, Ch. 1).

name: The ring class field of an order
text: for an order O of a number field K, the abelian extension L_O whose norm group is the kernel of the idele class group onto Pic O, with Pic O ≅ Gal(L_O/K) by the Artin map (Cox, *Primes of the Form x² + ny²*, Thm 9.18).

name: D-finite power series
text: a power series satisfying a linear differential equation with polynomial coefficients, equivalently one whose derivatives are linearly dependent over k[X]; closed under sums, products and derivatives (Stanley, *European J. Combin.* 1 (1980)).

name: The smooth noncommutative torus
text: the ⋆-algebra 𝒜_θ of rapidly decreasing series in two unitaries with U₂U₁ = e^{2πiθ}U₁U₂, with its faithful canonical trace (Connes, *Noncommutative Geometry*, IV.6).

name: Cellular algebras
text: an algebra with a basis indexed by a poset of cells and pairs of tableaux, compatible with an anti-involution, together with its lower-cell ideals, cell representations and Gram matrices (Graham–Lehrer, *Invent. Math.* 123 (1996), Def. 1.1).

name: The structure sheaf of the formal spectrum
text: for an adic ring A, the sheaf of rings lim 𝒪_{Spec(A/Jⁿ)} on Spf A, with global sections A when A is complete (EGA I, 10.1.2–10.1.3).

name: The R-transform
text: the formal R-transform R(z) = Σ κₙ₊₁ zⁿ of a noncommutative random variable, with C(zM(z)) = M(z) relating the moment and free cumulant series, and R_{a+b} = R_a + R_b for free a, b (Nica–Speicher, *Lectures on the Combinatorics of Free Probability*, 12 and 16).

name: Displacement interpolation
text: a curve of probability measures is a displacement interpolation when it is the family of time marginals of a dynamic plan on constant-speed geodesics whose endpoint law is an optimal coupling (Villani, *Optimal Transport: Old and New*, Ch. 7).

name: Warped products
text: the Riemannian metric g_M + f² g_N on M × N for a nowhere-vanishing warping function f on M, with the Bishop–O'Neill formula for its Levi-Civita connection (O'Neill, *Semi-Riemannian Geometry*, Ch. 7).

name: The Jacobi elliptic functions
text: the amplitude am(u, k), inverse of the incomplete integral F(φ, k), and sn = sin am, cn = cos am, dn = √(1 − k² sn²), with their derivatives and periods (DLMF, Ch. 22).

## What it says
`hφ.nakayamaAut` is the Nakayama automorphism of a Frobenius functional $\varphi$ on a finite-dimensional algebra: the $k$-algebra automorphism $\nu$ of $A$ with $\varphi(ab) = \varphi(b\,\nu(a))$ for all $a, b$.

- `{k : Type v} [Field k]`: a field $k$.
- `{A : Type u} [Ring A] [Algebra k A] [FiniteDimensional k A]`: a finite-dimensional associative $k$-algebra with $1$, not assumed commutative.

- Its type `A ≃ₐ[k] A`: a $k$-algebra automorphism of $A$.
- Its value: in finite dimension the form is a perfect pairing, so for each $a$ there is a unique $\nu(a)$ with $\varphi(b\,\nu(a)) = \varphi(ab)$ for all $b$; this $\nu$ is shown multiplicative, unital and injective, hence bijective.

This is the Nakayama automorphism of Lam, Section 16, and of Skowroński and Yamagata, in the normalisation $\varphi(ab) = \varphi(b\,\nu(a))$ that the roadmap fixes; `coe_nakayamaAut_eq` makes it independent of the construction.

## What it says
`groupAlgebraInvariantsCharacterEquiv rho` identifies the characters, over the splitting field $L$, of the group descended from the diagonalizable group $D(M)$ with $M$ itself: a group isomorphism from the group-like elements of $L \otimes_k B$ onto $M$ written multiplicatively.

- `[AddCommGroup M]`: an abelian group $M$, not assumed finitely generated or torsion-free.
- `(rho : Representation ℤ (L ≃ₐ[k] L) M)`: an action of $\mathrm{Gal}(L/k)$ on $M$ by automorphisms.
- `groupAlgebraInvariants rho`, written $B$: the $k$-subalgebra of $L[M]$ fixed by $\sigma \cdot (a X^m) = \sigma(a) X^{\rho(\sigma) m}$, the coordinate Hopf algebra of the descended group.
- Its type `GroupLike L (L ⊗[k] B) ≃* Multiplicative M`: the group-likes of the $L$-Hopf algebra $L \otimes_k B$, which are the characters $T_L \to \mathbb{G}_m$, are isomorphic as a group to $M$.

This is the first half of the classification of tori and diagonalizable groups by Galois lattices: over the splitting field, the character group of the descended group is the lattice one started from, and `groupAlgebraInvariantsCharacterEquiv_smul` says the Galois action on characters goes over to $\rho$.

## What it says
Weyl's theorem for algebraic groups: over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, every finite-dimensional representation of a connected affine group of finite type whose Lie algebra has nondegenerate Killing form is completely reducible.

- `{k : Type u} [Field k] [CharZero k] [IsAlgClosed k]`: an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero.
- `{H : FiniteTypeCommHopfAlgCat.{u, u} k}`: a finitely generated commutative Hopf algebra, the coordinate ring of an affine group $G$ of finite type.
- `[ConnectedSpace (PrimeSpectrum H)]`: $G$ is connected.
- `[LieAlgebra.IsKilling k (Derivation k H (Bialgebra.CounitAlgebra k H k))]`: $\mathrm{Lie}(G)$, the derivations of $H$ into $k$ through the counit, has nondegenerate Killing form; in characteristic zero, Cartan's criterion makes this semisimplicity.
- `{M : Type w} [AddCommGroup M] [Module k M] [Comodule k H M] [FiniteDimensional k M]`: a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space with a right $H$-comodule structure, a representation of $G$.
- The conclusion, `IsCompletelyReducible k H M`: every subcomodule of $M$ has a complementary subcomodule, so $M$ is a direct sum of irreducibles.

This is the linear reductivity in characteristic zero of a connected group with semisimple Lie algebra, Milne §22.42 and Humphreys §13. The proof differentiates $M$ to a $\mathrm{Lie}(G)$-module, applies Weyl's theorem, and uses that for connected $G$ in characteristic zero the $\mathrm{Lie}(G)$-stable subspaces are the subrepresentations (`isCompletelyReducible_iff_forall_differential_mem`).

## What it says
Over a perfect field $k$, the character-lattice functor is an equivalence of categories from the coordinate Hopf algebras of tori over $k$ to the continuous integral Galois lattices of $k$. On the group schemes this is the classical anti-equivalence between tori and Galois lattices.

- `{k : Type u} [Field k] [PerfectField k]`: a perfect field.
- The instance provides `(characterLatticeFunctor (k := k)).IsEquivalence`: the functor `characterLatticeFunctor : TorusCommHopfAlgCat k ⥤ GaloisLatticeCat k` is fully faithful and essentially surjective.
- Its source, `TorusCommHopfAlgCat k`: the finitely generated commutative Hopf algebras over $k$ that become coordinate rings of split tori of finite rank after base change to an algebraic closure, the coordinate rings of tori, split or not; morphisms are Hopf algebra maps, so this is the opposite of the category of tori.
- Its target, `GaloisLatticeCat k`: integral representations of $\Gamma = \mathrm{Gal}(\bar k/k)$ on finite free $\mathbb{Z}$-modules in which every vector has an open stabiliser, that is continuous for the discrete topology, with equivariant linear maps.
- The functor sends a torus $T$ to $X^*(T) = \mathrm{Hom}_{\bar k}(T_{\bar k}, \mathbb{G}_m)$, the group-likes of $\bar k \otimes_k \mathcal{O}(T)$ written additively, with $\Gamma$ acting through the scalar factor.

This is Milne's Theorem 12.23 and Corollary 12.24, the classification of tori by character lattices with Galois action, stated for perfect fields: the file says perfectness is used only to descend from the algebraic closure, which then is the separable closure. The variance is covariant because the objects are coordinate rings.

## What it says
A reduced affine group of finite type over an algebraically closed field is geometrically unipotent if and only if it embeds as a closed subgroup scheme of some upper-unitriangular group $U_n$.

- `{k H : Type u} [Field k] [CommRing H] [HopfAlgebra k H]`: a field and a commutative Hopf algebra over it, the coordinate ring of $G = \mathrm{Spec}\,H$.
- `[IsAlgClosed k]`: $k$ is algebraically closed.
- `[Algebra.FiniteType k H]`: $G$ is of finite type.
- `[IsReduced H]`: $G$ is reduced, a variety; over an algebraically closed field this is smoothness.
- The left side, `geometricallyUnipotentPointsCommHopfAlgProperty k (CommHopfAlgCat.of k H)`: every point of $G$ with values in an algebraic closure of $k$ acts by a unipotent linear map on the scalar extension of every finite-dimensional representation.
- The right side: there are $n$ and a homomorphism $f$ of group schemes over $\mathrm{Spec}\,k$ from $G$, `hopfSpec` applied to $H$, to `UpperUnitriangular.groupScheme k (Fin n)`, the group $U_n$ of upper-triangular matrices with ones on the diagonal, whose underlying morphism of schemes `f.hom.hom.left` is a closed immersion.

This is the closed-subgroup form of the theorem that a group of unipotent matrices is conjugate into $U_n$: Springer's Proposition 2.4.12 and Borel §4.8 with its Corollary. The forward direction is Kolchin's fixed-vector theorem on a faithful finite-dimensional subcomodule of the regular representation; the converse holds because the points of $U_n$ are unipotent and unipotence passes to closed subgroups. Unlike the roadmap's formulation for smooth connected groups, no connectedness is assumed, as in the classical statement.

## What it says
`IsAlgebraicSpace F` says that a presheaf of sets `F` on the category of schemes is an *algebraic space* in the sense of the Stacks Project: an fppf sheaf whose diagonal is representable by schemes and which has an étale atlas.

- `(F : SchemePresheaf)`: a presheaf of sets on schemes, `Scheme.{u}ᵒᵖ ⥤ Type u`, such as the functor of points `h_X = yoneda.obj X` of a scheme `X`.
- It is a `structure ... : Prop`, a proposition with three fields, all required.
  - `isSheaf`: `F` is a sheaf for `Scheme.fppfTopology`, Mathlib's topology on schemes generated by the jointly surjective families of flat morphisms locally of finite presentation.
  - `representableDiagonal`: `RepresentableDiagonal F`, that is `yoneda.relativelyRepresentable (diag F)`: for every scheme `T` and morphism `h_T ⟶ F ⨯ F`, its fibre product with the diagonal `F ⟶ F ⨯ F` is represented by a scheme. By Mathlib's `Functor.relativelyRepresentable.diag_iff`, this says that every morphism `h_U ⟶ F` from a scheme is representable.
  - `exists_etaleAtlas`: there are a scheme `U` and a morphism `a : h_U ⟶ F` with `EtaleAtlas a`, that is `MorphismProperty.presheaf @Etale a` and `MorphismProperty.presheaf @Surjective a`: `a` is representable, and its base change along every `h_T ⟶ F` from a scheme is an étale, respectively surjective, morphism of schemes.

This is Definition 65.6.1 of the Stacks Project condition by condition: (1) the fppf sheaf condition, (2) the representable diagonal, (3) a surjective étale morphism from a scheme, "surjective" and "étale" for a transformation meaning, as there, representable with all base changes so. The one difference is the base: the Stacks Project works over a base scheme $S$; here the site is the category of all schemes, as the roadmap target asks.

`W.pointEquivDegreeZeroDivisorClass` is an isomorphism of abelian groups between the rational points of a Weierstrass curve $W$ over a field $F$ and the degree-zero divisor classes of its function field $F(W)$, the group $\mathrm{Cl}^0(F(W))$, which is $\mathrm{Pic}^0$ of the curve over $F$.

- `{F : Type u_1} [Field F]`: a field $F$.
- `(W : WeierstrassCurve.Affine F)`: a Weierstrass curve over $F$, in affine form.
- `[IsDedekindDomain W.CoordinateRing]`: the affine coordinate ring $F[x, y]/(\text{Weierstrass equation})$ is a Dedekind domain, the nonsingularity of the affine curve. Tau Ceti supplies it from `[W.IsElliptic]` (`isDedekindDomain_coordinateRing`).
- `[DecidableEq F]`: Mathlib's hypothesis for the group law on `W.Point`.
- The type `W.Point ≃+ (Divisor.degreeClass W.isFunctionField).ker`: on the left Mathlib's group of $F$-rational points, the point at infinity `0` and the nonsingular affine points `some x y h`. On the right, `W.isFunctionField` is the proof that $F(W)$ is a function field of one variable over $F$; `(Place.orderSystem W.isFunctionField).ClassGroup` is its divisor class group, Weil divisors on the places of $F(W)/F$ modulo principal divisors; `Divisor.degreeClass` is the degree on classes, each place counted with its degree $[\kappa(P) : F]$; `.ker` is the classes of degree $0$.
- Its value: `Point.toClassEquiv`, which sends a point to its class in the ideal class group of the coordinate ring, the point at infinity to the trivial class and $(x, y)$ to the class of $(X - x, Y - y)$, composed with the inverse of `Divisor.degreeZeroClassGroupEquiv`, which identifies $\mathrm{Cl}^0(F(W))$ with that ideal class group by restriction to the affine chart. The restriction is an isomorphism because the place at infinity is the only place infinite on the coordinate ring (`setOf_exists_notMem_integers_eq_singleton_infinity`) and is rational (`Place.degree_infinity`).

So an affine point $P$ goes to the class of $(P) - (O)$ and the point at infinity to the trivial class (`val_pointEquivDegreeZeroDivisorClass_some`). This is the map $\kappa : E \to \mathrm{Pic}^0(E)$, $P \mapsto [(P) - (O)]$, of Silverman, Proposition III.3.4, and the statement that it is a group isomorphism. Silverman works over an algebraically closed field; here the field is arbitrary, the points are the $F$-rational ones and the divisors those of $F(W)/F$, with places of every degree.

The $F$-automorphisms of the function field $F(W)$ of an elliptic curve that fix the place at infinity are exactly the automorphisms of the elliptic curve, acting on functions by substitution.

This is the identification $\mathrm{Aut}(E, O) = $ the changes of variables fixing the Weierstrass equation, as in Silverman, III.3 (isomorphisms of Weierstrass curves are changes of variables) and III.10 (automorphisms of an elliptic curve), read on the function field: an automorphism of $F(W)/F$ fixing the place at infinity restricts to a degree-one isogeny of $W$ to itself, which is a change of variables, and conversely a change of variables fixes $O$. The file's header gives the corresponding exercise of Stichtenoth. The statement is over the ground field $F$, not its algebraic closure: both sides consist of $F$-automorphisms.

## What it says
A complex in an abelian category whose cycles split off its terms, and whose homology splits off its cycles, is chain homotopy equivalent to a complex with zero differentials. Over a field, or more generally for a complex of semisimple modules, both splittings are automatic, so every such complex is homotopy equivalent to its homology.

- `{C : Type u_1} [Category C]`: a category $C$; `u_1` is a universe level, which does not affect the mathematics.
- `{ι : Type u_2} {c : ComplexShape ι}`: the index type of the complex and its shape, which says which pairs of degrees $j \to i$ carry a differential.
- `[Abelian C]`: $C$ is abelian, so kernels, cokernels, cycles and homology exist.
- `(K : HomologicalComplex C c)`: a complex $K$ of that shape in $C$.
- `[∀ i, IsSplitMono (K.iCycles i)]`: in every degree $i$ the inclusion $Z_i \to K_i$ of the cycles has a retraction $K_i \to Z_i$.
- `[∀ i, IsSplitEpi (K.homologyπ i)]`: in every degree $i$ the projection $Z_i \to H_i$ of the cycles onto the homology has a section $H_i \to Z_i$.
- The conclusion: there is a complex $L$ of the same shape in $C$ with every differential $L_i \to L_j$ equal to $0$, and a chain homotopy equivalence (`HomotopyEquiv`, Mathlib's: chain maps both ways whose composites are chain homotopic to the identities) between $K$ and $L$.

This is the classical splitting of a complex into its homology: choose a retraction $r$ of $Z_i \to K_i$ and a section $s$ of $Z_i \to H_i$; then $r \circ \pi$ and $s \circ \iota$ are chain maps between $K$ and the complex of homology objects with zero differential, homotopy inverse to each other. The theorem states only the existence of $L$; its terms are the homology of $K$, which a reader recovers from the equivalence by `HomotopyEquiv.toHomologyIso`, as the docstring says. The hypotheses are exactly the two splittings the classical argument uses, and no projectivity or finiteness is asked.

## What it says
The Harish-Chandra projection $Z(U(\mathfrak{g})) \to S(\mathfrak{h})$ is injective: a central element of the universal enveloping algebra of a split semisimple Lie algebra in characteristic zero is determined by its image in the symmetric algebra of the Cartan subalgebra.

- `{K : Type} [Field K] [CharZero K]`: a field $K$ of characteristic zero.
- `{L : Type v} [LieRing L] [LieAlgebra K L]`: a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g} = L$ over $K$.
- `[IsKilling K L]`: the Killing form of $L$ is non-degenerate; in characteristic zero this is the same as $L$ semisimple.
- `[FiniteDimensional K L]`: $L$ is finite-dimensional.
- `{H : LieSubalgebra K L} [H.IsCartanSubalgebra] [LieModule.IsTriangularizable K H L]`: a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak{h} = H$ that is splitting, that is, $L$ decomposes into weight spaces for $H$ over $K$.
- `(b : (IsKilling.rootSystem H).Base)`: a base, a set of simple roots, of the root system of $L$ relative to $H$. It fixes the positive roots, hence the triangular decomposition through which the projection is defined.
- The conclusion: `TauCeti.hcProjection b`, the $K$-algebra map from `Subalgebra.center K (UniversalEnvelopingAlgebra K L)` to `SymmetricAlgebra K H`, is an injective function.

`hcProjection b` is the restriction to the centre of the projection $U(\mathfrak{g}) \to U(\mathfrak{h}) \simeq S(\mathfrak{h})$ along the triangular decomposition, with no $\rho$-shift; its value at a weight $\lambda$ is the central character $\chi_\lambda$ of the Verma module $M(\lambda)$. Injectivity is one half of the Harish-Chandra isomorphism $Z(U(\mathfrak{g})) \simeq S(\mathfrak{h})^{W\cdot}$; Humphreys proves it in §23.3 for a semisimple Lie algebra over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, by comparing the PBW filtration of the centre with the degree filtration of $S(\mathfrak{h})$ through Chevalley's restriction theorem, and the file follows that argument. The statement here is for any split semisimple Lie algebra over any field of characteristic zero, which contains Humphreys's case.

## What it says
Thom's lemma for roots: a root of a nonzero polynomial over an ordered field with polynomial Rolle is determined by the signs of its derivatives of orders $1, \dots, \deg p$ at that root. Two roots with the same finite Thom encoding are equal, with no squarefreeness asked of $p$.

- `{R : Type u_1} [Field R] [LinearOrder R] [IsStrictOrderedRing R]`: an ordered field $R$, that is, a field with a linear order compatible with its operations.
- `(p : R[X])`: a polynomial $p$ over $R$.
- `(hrolle : TauCeti.PolynomialRolle R)`: polynomial Rolle holds in $R$: whenever a polynomial takes equal values at $a < b$, its formal derivative has a root strictly between them. Every real closed field has this property (`TauCeti.RealClosure.polynomialRolle_of_isRealClosed`); it is the only analytic input.
- `(hp : p ≠ 0)`: $p$ is not the zero polynomial.
- The conclusion: `Set.InjOn (thomEncoding p) {x | p.eval x = 0}`: the map $x \mapsto \mathrm{thomEncoding}(p, x)$ is injective on the set of roots of $p$. Here `thomEncoding p x : Fin p.natDegree → SignType` is the list of the signs ($-1$, $0$ or $1$) of $p^{(k)}(x)$ for $k = 1, \dots, \deg p$.

This is the consequence of Thom's lemma in Basu, Pollack and Roy, Proposition 2.28: over a real closed field, a root of $p$ is characterised among the roots of $p$ by the sign condition it realises on the derivatives of $p$. The statement here asks only an ordered field in which polynomial Rolle holds, which is more general than a real closed field, and the proof is the usual one: sign conditions on all derivatives are convex on intervals, so two distinct points with the same encoding would force $p$ to vanish on a whole interval.

## What it says
Ocneanu's theorem: on the infinite type-A Hecke algebra over any commutative ring, for every value $z$ of the parameter there is exactly one Markov trace with parameter $z$.

- `{R : Type*} [CommRing R]`: a commutative ring $R$ of coefficients.
- `{q : Rˣ}`: a unit $q$ of $R$, the Hecke parameter. `InfiniteTypeAHeckeAlgebra R q` is the $R$-algebra on generators $T_0, T_1, \dots$ with $T_i^2 = (q - q^{-1})T_i + 1$, the braid relations $T_iT_{i+1}T_i = T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}$ and $T_iT_j = T_jT_i$ for $|i - j| \ge 2$; it is the union of its stages $H_n$, the subalgebra generated by $T_0, \dots, T_{n-2}$, the image of the Hecke algebra on $n$ strands.
- `(z : R)`: the Markov parameter.
- The conclusion, `∃! τ : InfiniteTypeAHeckeAlgebra R q →ₗ[R] R, IsMarkovTrace z τ`: there is a unique $R$-linear functional $\tau$ on the algebra with the three properties of `IsMarkovTrace z`: $\tau(1) = 1$; $\tau(xy) = \tau(yx)$ for all $x, y$; and the Markov rule $\tau(x T_n) = z\,\tau(x)$ whenever $x$ lies in the stage $H_{n+1}$ of the first $n + 1$ strands.

This is Theorem 5.1 of Jones, where the trace is built one strand at a time and shown unique by the decomposition $H_{n+2} = H_{n+1} + H_{n+1}T_nH_{n+1}$, in the Jimbo normalisation $T^2 = (q - q^{-1})T + 1$ of the quadratic relation rather than Jones's $(T - q)(T + 1) = 0$. Existence is `isMarkovTrace_ocneanuTrace`, with `ocneanuTrace R q z` as witness, and uniqueness is `IsMarkovTrace.unique`. Only the algebraic statement is made: no positivity is claimed.

This is the standard description of $\mathfrak{g}_2$ as $\mathfrak{sl}_3 \oplus W \oplus W^*$ with its root-space decomposition, as in Fulton and Harris, Lecture 22, and of $\mathrm{Der}$ of a Cayley algebra as the Lie algebra of type $G_2$, as in Schafer, Chapter III. The literature works over $\mathbb{C}$; here any commutative ring with $2$ and $3$ invertible is allowed, the invertibility being what makes the raising and lowering generators generate.

## What it says
A morphism of schemes over a field from a proper geometrically integral monoid scheme to a separated group scheme locally of finite type is a homomorphism as soon as it preserves the identity. For abelian varieties this is the corollary of the rigidity lemma: a morphism with $f(0) = 0$ is a homomorphism.

- `{K : Type u} [Field K]`: a field $K$.
- `{A B : Over (Spec (.of K))}`: two schemes $A$, $B$ with structure morphisms to $\operatorname{Spec} K$; this category is cartesian monoidal, its product being the fibre product over $\operatorname{Spec} K$.
- `[MonObj A]`: a monoid structure on $A$ in that category, a unit $\eta : \operatorname{Spec} K \to A$ and a multiplication $\mu : A \times_K A \to A$ with the monoid axioms; `[GrpObj B]`: a group structure on $B$, a monoid structure with an inverse.
- `[IsProper A.hom] [GeometricallyIntegral A.hom]`: $A$ is proper over $K$, and $A \times_K \operatorname{Spec} L$ is integral for every field extension $L$ of $K$.
- `[IsSeparated B.hom] [LocallyOfFiniteType B.hom]`: $B$ is separated and locally of finite type over $K$.
- `(f : A ⟶ B)`: a morphism over $\operatorname{Spec} K$; `(hf : η[A] ≫ f = η[B])`: it sends the identity of $A$ to the identity of $B$.
- The conclusion, `IsMonHom f`: $f$ is a morphism of monoid objects, that is, it preserves the unit and $\mu_A \circ f = (f \times f) \circ \mu_B$ in the usual diagrammatic order, so $f(xy) = f(x)f(y)$ on points.

Mumford states this for abelian varieties, as Corollary 1 to the rigidity lemma in Section 4, and Milne as Corollary 1.2; both allow a translation, which the hypothesis $f(0) = 0$ removes. The statement here is more general in the same way as the rigidity lemma it rests on, `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.eq_snd_comp_lift_comp`: the source need only be a proper geometrically integral monoid scheme, and the target any separated group scheme locally of finite type, not necessarily commutative, since the defect $f(xy)\,(f(x)f(y))^{-1}$ is formed in the group of morphisms into $B$. The same file deduces that homomorphisms of abelian varieties are exactly the pointed morphisms of their underlying schemes, `AbelianVariety.Hom.equivPointed`.

## What it says
This instance records that the translations form a normal subgroup of the group of $F$-automorphisms of the function field $F(W)$ of an elliptic curve $W$.

- `{F : Type u_1} [Field F]`: a field $F$.
- `(W : WeierstrassCurve.Affine F) [W.IsElliptic]`: a Weierstrass curve over $F$ whose discriminant is a unit, that is, an elliptic curve.
- `[DecidableEq F]`: Mathlib's hypothesis for the group law on the points.
- `translationHom W` is the action of the point group on the function field: the monoid homomorphism from `Multiplicative (W⁄F).toAffine.Point`, the group of rational points written multiplicatively, to `W.FunctionField ≃ₐ[F] W.FunctionField`, the $F$-algebra automorphisms of $F(W)$, sending a point $P$ to `translation W P`, the pullback $\tau_P^*$ of the translation $Q \mapsto Q + P$ of the curve, which on the coordinate ring is evaluation at the translate of the generic point.
- `(translationHom W).range` is its image, the subgroup $T = \{\tau_P^* : P \in W(F)\}$.
- The conclusion, `.Normal`: for every $\tau \in T$ and every automorphism $\sigma$ of $F(W)/F$, $\sigma \tau \sigma^{-1} \in T$.

This is the standard structure of the automorphism group of a genus-one function field with a rational point: $\mathrm{Aut}(F(W)/F)$ is the semidirect product of the translations by the automorphisms of the elliptic curve $(W, O)$, so the translations are normal. The file proves it from the complement `isComplement'_stabilizer_infinity_range_translationHom` and the fact that an automorphism of the curve conjugates $\tau_P^*$ to a translation (`exists_autGroupToAlgEquiv_mul_translation_mul_inv_eq`), the translations commuting among themselves.

## References and tests
- H. Stichtenoth, *Algebraic Function Fields and Codes*, 2nd ed., Exercise 6.14 (the reference the file gives for the structure of $\mathrm{Aut}(F(W)/F)$).
- J. Silverman, *The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves*, III.3 and III.10, for translations and the automorphisms of an elliptic curve.
- `WeierstrassCurve.Affine.exists_autGroupToAlgEquiv_mul_translation_mul_inv_eq` — the special case of conjugation by the automorphism of a change of variables fixing $W$: it carries a translation to a translation.
- `WeierstrassCurve.Affine.quotientRangeTranslationHomMulEquiv` — the quotient by this normal subgroup is the automorphism group of the elliptic curve, $\mathrm{Aut}(F(W)/F)/T \cong \mathrm{Aut}(E, O)$, which is what the normality is for.

The special case is the whole content: every automorphism is an automorphism of the curve followed by a translation, and translations commute, so conjugation by the curve automorphisms is all that has to be checked.

## Lean subtleties
- It is an `instance`: Lean finds the normality by itself whenever it needs the quotient group `(W.FunctionField ≃ₐ[F] W.FunctionField) ⧸ (translationHom W).range`.
- `(W⁄F)` is the base change of $W$ to $F$ itself, the form in which the translation action is stated; `Point.equivBaseChangeSelf` identifies its points with those of $W$.
- `Multiplicative` is a type wrapper that writes the additive point group multiplicatively, so that `translationHom` can be a monoid homomorphism into a group of automorphisms; `Multiplicative.ofAdd P` is the point $P$ seen there.
- The codomain of `translationHom` is printed `Gal(W.FunctionField/F)`. This is Mathlib's notation for `W.FunctionField ≃ₐ[F] W.FunctionField`, the group of all $F$-algebra automorphisms of the field $F(W)$, and carries no claim that $F(W)/F$ is a Galois extension: $F(W)/F$ is transcendental, and the group is simply $\mathrm{Aut}(F(W)/F)$.
- The automorphisms are `≃ₐ[F]`, $F$-algebra automorphisms of the whole function field, not automorphisms of the curve; the statement is about all of $\mathrm{Aut}(F(W)/F)$.

## What it says
`TauCeti.Quaternion.brauerGroupMulEquiv` is an isomorphism of groups between the Brauer group of the real numbers and the cyclic group of order two: $\mathrm{Br}(\mathbb{R}) \cong \mathbb{Z}/2$, with the class of the Hamilton quaternions $\mathbb{H}$ as the generator.

- Its type, `BrauerGroup.{0, 0} ℝ ≃* Multiplicative (ZMod 2)`: a group isomorphism from `BrauerGroup ℝ`, the Brauer classes of finite-dimensional central simple $\mathbb{R}$-algebras with the group law induced by the tensor product (`TauCeti.BrauerGroup.instCommGroup`), to $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ written multiplicatively.
- Its value: the inverse of Mathlib's `zmodMulEquivOfGenerator`, fed the facts that the class of $\mathbb{H}$ generates the group (`TauCeti.Quaternion.zpowers_mk_eq_top`) and that the group has exactly two elements (`TauCeti.Quaternion.card_brauerGroup_eq_two`). So the class of $\mathbb{H}$ goes to the generator `Multiplicative.ofAdd 1`, and the identity, the class of $\mathbb{R}$ or of any $M_n(\mathbb{R})$, to the identity.

This is the classical computation $\mathrm{Br}(\mathbb{R}) = \mathbb{Z}/2$, a consequence of Frobenius' theorem that $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{H}$ are the only finite-dimensional central division algebras over $\mathbb{R}$. Two-element groups have a unique isomorphism between them, so the isomorphism is the canonical one.

The target lists no Checks.

- `TauCeti.Quaternion.brauerGroupMulEquiv_symm_ofAdd_one` — its inverse sends the generator back to the class of $\mathbb{H}$.

The two lemmas pin the isomorphism down on the generator, so it is the one the roadmap asks for.

- `BrauerGroup ℝ` is Mathlib's quotient of the bundled central simple algebras `CSA ℝ` by Brauer equivalence (isomorphic after passing to matrix algebras); the group structure is Tau Ceti's, induced by $\otimes_\mathbb{R}$, with the class of $\mathbb{R}$ as identity and the opposite algebra as inverse.
- `BrauerGroup.{0, 0} ℝ` pins the universe levels to `Type`, where $\mathbb{R}$ lives and where the group law is defined.
- `Multiplicative (ZMod 2)` is $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ with its addition read as multiplication; `Multiplicative.ofAdd 1` is the generator.
- The definition is `noncomputable`: it comes from an abstract isomorphism of cyclic groups, so Lean cannot evaluate it; its values are fixed by the two lemmas above.
- `ℍ[ℝ]` is Mathlib's `Quaternion ℝ`, with $i^2 = j^2 = -1$; `CSA.of ℝ ℍ[ℝ]` bundles it with its central, simple and finite-dimensional instances.

## What it says
`TauCeti.CellularBasis R A M` is the structure of a **cellular basis**, or cell datum, on an algebra $A$ in the sense of Graham and Lehrer: the data making $A$ a cellular algebra.

Its parameters are implicit: `R` with `[CommRing R]`, a commutative ring; `A` with `[Ring A] [Algebra R A]`, an associative unital $R$-algebra; `Λ` with `[Preorder Λ]`, the cells; `M : Λ → Type*` with `[∀ μ, Fintype (M μ)]`, a finite index set $M(\mu)$ for each cell.

Its fields:
- `basis`: an $R$-basis of $A$ indexed by the triples $(\mu, s, t)$ with $\mu \in \Lambda$ and $s, t \in M(\mu)$: the vectors $C^\mu_{s,t}$.
- `antiInvolution`: an $R$-algebra isomorphism $A \cong A^{\mathrm{op}}$, that is an $R$-linear anti-automorphism $a \mapsto a^*$.
- `unop_antiInvolution_basis`: $(C^\mu_{s,t})^* = C^\mu_{t,s}$.
- `exists_mul_basis`: for every $a \in A$, $\mu$ and $s$ there are coefficients $r(u) \in R$ such that for every $t$, $a\, C^\mu_{s,t} - \sum_u r(u)\, C^\mu_{u,t}$ lies in the span $A(<\mu)$ of the basis vectors of the cells $\nu < \mu$. The coefficients do not depend on $t$.

These are (C1), (C2) and (C3) of Graham and Lehrer's Definition 1.1. The differences: the cells form any preorder rather than a finite poset; that $*$ squares to the identity is not asked, since it follows from its values on the basis (`TauCeti.CellularBasis.unop_antiInvolution_unop_antiInvolution`); and the coefficients are not data, since the basis determines them (`TauCeti.CellularBasis.cellRep`).

- `TauCeti.CellularBasis.gramMatrix_matrix` — in that example the Gram matrix of the single cell is the identity.

The matrix algebra is the simplest cellular algebra of the paper; that it fits the fields shows they carry the intended content.

## Lean subtleties
- `Basis (Σ μ, M μ × M μ) R A` is an $R$-module basis indexed by a dependent sum, written `⟨μ, s, t⟩`.
- `A ≃ₐ[R] Aᵐᵒᵖ` is an isomorphism to the multiplicative opposite; `.unop` reads its value back in $A$. This is how an anti-automorphism is expressed.
- `i.1 < μ` is the strict order of the preorder: $\nu \le \mu$ and not $\mu \le \nu$.
- `span R (basis '' …)` is the submodule $A(<\mu)$; that it is a two-sided ideal is a theorem, not a field.
- `∃ r, ∀ t, …`: the quantifier order is what makes the coefficients independent of $t$.
- With `Λ` empty, $A$ is the zero algebra, which the definition allows.

## What it says
A finite-dimensional central division algebra $D$ over a field $K$ has a separable maximal subfield: a finite separable extension $L/K$ embedded in $D$, of degree the degree of $D$, and $L$ splits $D$.

- `(K : Type*) [Field K]`: any field, perfect or not.
- `(D : Type u) [DivisionRing D] [Algebra K D]`: a division ring that is a $K$-algebra.
- `[Algebra.IsCentral K D]`: the centre of $D$ is $K$; `[FiniteDimensional K D]`: $\dim_K D < \infty$.
- The conclusion: there are a type `L` with a field structure and a $K$-algebra structure, and a $K$-algebra map `L →ₐ[K] D`, so $L$ is a subfield of $D$ over $K$; such that $L/K$ is finite, `Algebra.IsSeparable K L` (every element of $L$ is separable over $K$), $[L:K]$ equals `deg K D`, the degree $\sqrt{\dim_K D}$ of $D$; and `IsSplittingField K D L`, that is $L \otimes_K D \cong M_n(L)$ as $L$-algebras for some $n$.

This is the classical theorem that a central division algebra over any field has a separable maximal subfield, which then splits it: the separable refinement of "a maximal subfield of degree $\deg D$ splits $D$", and the step giving a central simple algebra over an imperfect field a finite separable splitting field. It is stated for division algebras, as $[L:K] = \deg D$ requires; a general central simple algebra reduces to its division-algebra representative.

## What it says
`TauCeti.CrossedProduct c` is the **crossed-product algebra** $(L, G, c)$ of a $2$-cocycle $c$ of $G = \mathrm{Aut}_K(L)$ with values in $L^\times$: the free $L$-module on symbols $u_\sigma$, $\sigma \in G$, with $u_\sigma x = \sigma(x) u_\sigma$ and $u_\sigma u_\tau = c(\sigma, \tau) u_{\sigma\tau}$.

- Its parameters: `K` with `[CommSemiring K]`; `L` with `[CommRing L] [Algebra K L]`, a commutative $K$-algebra; `(c : TwoCocycle K L)`, a function $c(\sigma, \tau) \in L^\times$ on pairs of $K$-automorphisms of $L$ with $c(\sigma\tau, \rho)\, c(\sigma, \tau) = \sigma(c(\tau, \rho))\, c(\sigma, \tau\rho)$, Mathlib's `IsMulCocycle₂`.
- Its one field, `toFinsupp : (L ≃ₐ[K] L) →₀ L`: the coordinates $\sigma \mapsto a_\sigma$ of $\sum_\sigma a_\sigma u_\sigma$, finitely supported; `ofFinsupp` builds the element from them.

The structure is a wrapper; its meaning is in the instances of the same file: the $L$-basis `CrossedProduct.basis c` of the $u_\sigma$, the product $(x u_\sigma)(y u_\tau) = (x\, \sigma(y)\, c(\sigma, \tau))\, u_{\sigma\tau}$ extended biadditively, the identity $c(1,1)^{-1} u_1$, a `Ring` and a $K$-algebra structure, and the embedding `CrossedProduct.inc c` of $L$, $x \mapsto x\, c(1,1)^{-1} u_1$. The cocycle identity is exactly associativity.

This is the crossed product of Gille–Szamuely §4.4 and Serre's *Local Fields*, Chapter X, with the same rules, stated more generally: $G$ is all of $\mathrm{Aut}_K(L)$, $K$ a commutative semiring, $L$ a commutative ring, and the cocycle not necessarily normalised. For a finite Galois extension of fields it has dimension $[L:K]^2$ and is central simple (`TauCeti.Algebra.CrossedProduct.CentralSimple`).

The target lists no Checks.

- `TauCeti.CrossedProduct.basis_mul_inc` and `TauCeti.CrossedProduct.basis_mul_basis` — the rules $u_\sigma x = \sigma(x) u_\sigma$ and $u_\sigma u_\tau = c(\sigma,\tau) u_{\sigma\tau}$.

- `(L ≃ₐ[K] L) →₀ L` is finitely supported: finitely many nonzero coordinates even when $\mathrm{Aut}_K(L)$ is infinite.
- `L ≃ₐ[K] L` is the group of all $K$-automorphisms of $L$, the Galois group only when $L/K$ is Galois; the construction does not assume that.
- The crossed product is a $K$-algebra and a left $L$-module, not an $L$-algebra: $L$ is not central unless the group is trivial.
- The identity is $c(1,1)^{-1} u_1$, not $u_1$, since the cocycle need not be normalised.
- The ring structure is `noncomputable`, built through the basis and finite sums.

## What it says
`TauCeti.CrossedSystem.Algebra c` is the **crossed product with noncommutative coefficients** of a normalised crossed system $c = (D, \sigma, a)$: the free left $D$-module on symbols $[g]$, $g \in G$, with $(d[g])(e[h]) = d\, \sigma_g(e)\, a(g,h)\, [gh]$.

- Its parameters: `k` with `[CommSemiring k]`, the central base; `D` with `[Semiring D] [Algebra k D]`, the coefficient algebra, not assumed commutative; `G` with `[Monoid G]`; and `(c : CrossedSystem k D G)`: $k$-algebra automorphisms $\sigma_g$ of $D$ and units $a(g,h) \in D^\times$ with $\sigma_1 = \mathrm{id}$, $a(1,g) = a(g,1) = 1$, the twisted action law $\sigma_g(\sigma_h(d))\, a(g,h) = a(g,h)\, \sigma_{gh}(d)$, that is $\sigma_g \sigma_h = \mathrm{Ad}(a(g,h))\, \sigma_{gh}$, and the cocycle law $a(g,h)\, a(gh,j) = \sigma_g(a(h,j))\, a(g,hj)$.
- Its one field, `toFinsupp : G →₀ D`: the coefficients $g \mapsto d_g$ of $\sum_g d_g [g]$, finitely supported; `ofFinsupp` builds the element from them.

The structure is a wrapper; its meaning is in the instances of the file: the $D$-basis `basis c` of the $[g]$, the product above, the identity $[1]$, `Semiring` and (for a ring $D$) `Ring` structures, a $k$-algebra structure, and the injective, non-central embedding `inc c`, $d \mapsto d[1]$. The two laws are exactly associativity.

This is the crossed product of a group over a ring with a twisted action and factor set, as in Karpilovsky, in normalised form, with $\sigma$ an action only up to inner automorphisms. It is the algebra Clifford theory over non-splitting fields needs, where $D$ is a division algebra of equivariant endomorphisms.

## What it says
For a finite Galois extension $L/K$, the Brauer class of the crossed product of the pointwise product of two $2$-cocycles is the product of their Brauer classes: $[(L, G, cd)] = [(L, G, c)] \cdot [(L, G, d)]$ in $\mathrm{Br}(K)$.

- `{K : Type u} [Field K]`, `{L : Type u} [Field L] [Algebra K L]`: fields $K \subseteq L$ in the same universe.
- `[FiniteDimensional K L] [IsGalois K L]`: $L/K$ finite Galois, so $G = \mathrm{Aut}_K(L)$ is its Galois group.
- `(c d : TwoCocycle K L)`: $2$-cocycles of $G$ in $L^\times$, with the identity $c(\sigma\tau,\rho)\,c(\sigma,\tau) = \sigma(c(\tau,\rho))\,c(\sigma,\tau\rho)$.
- The conclusion: `crossedProductClass (c * d) = crossedProductClass c * crossedProductClass d`, where `c * d` is the pointwise product, `crossedProductClass c` is the class in `BrauerGroup K` of the central simple algebra `CrossedProduct c`, and the product on the right is the Brauer group law, the class of the tensor product over $K$.

This is the multiplicativity of the map from cocycles to Brauer classes, the step making $H^2(G, L^\times) \to \mathrm{Br}(L/K)$ a homomorphism, as in Gille–Szamuely §4.4 and Serre's *Local Fields*, Chapter X. It is stated for cocycles, not classes; that cohomologous cocycles give the same class is a separate statement. The proof is the standard $(L,G,c) \otimes_K (L,G,d) \cong M_{|G|}((L,G,cd))$.

## What it says
`TauCeti.AInfinityAlgebra.transfer` is the **homotopy transfer** of an $A_\infty$ structure along a special contraction: from an $A_\infty$ algebra $\mathcal{A}$ on $A$ and a strong deformation retract of $(A, m_1)$ onto a graded module $(H, d_H)$, it produces the transferred $A_\infty$ structure on $H$.

- `{R} [CommRing R]`, `{A} {H}` with `[AddCommGroup _] [Module R _]`: a commutative ring and two modules.
- `(𝒜 : AInfinityAlgebra R A)`: an $A_\infty$ algebra on $A$, cohomologically graded, with operations $m_n$ of degree $2 - n$ and $m_0 = 0$.
- `{GH : InternalGrading R H} {dH : Module.End R H}`: the grading of $H$ and the differential of the retract, implicit.
- `(c : LinearSpecialContraction 𝒜.differential dH)`: maps $i : H \to A$, $p : A \to H$, $h : A \to A$ with $i$, $p$ chain maps, $p i = 1$, $1 - ip = dh + hd$, and the side conditions $hi = 0$, $ph = 0$, $h^2 = 0$.
- `(hh) (hincl) (hproj)`: $h$ has degree $-1$, and $i$, $p$ degree $0$.
- Its value: the $A_\infty$ algebra on $H$ whose Taylor map is the letter component of the perturbed bar differential $D' = D + pXi$ on the tensor coalgebra of $sH$, with $X = (1 + \delta K)^{-1}\delta$: the basic perturbation lemma applied to the tensor-trick contraction of the bar constructions, along the higher part $\delta$ of the bar differential of $\mathcal{A}$ (`TauCeti.AInfinityAlgebra.transferBarDifferential`).

This is the construction of Gugenheim–Lambe–Stasheff, and it agrees with the tree formulas: $m_1 = d_H$, $m_2 = p\, m_2 (i \otimes i)$, and the Kontsevich–Soibelman/Merkulov $m_3 = p m_3 (i\otimes i\otimes i) + p m_2(h m_2(i \otimes i) \otimes i) - p m_2(i \otimes h m_2(i \otimes i))$ with the Koszul sign. When $d_H = 0$ the structure is minimal: the input to Kadeishvili's theorem.

- B. Keller, *Introduction to A-infinity algebras and modules*, Section 3.3; M. Kontsevich, Y. Soibelman, *Homological mirror symmetry and torus fibrations*, Section 6.4, for the tree formulas.

The target lists no Checks.
- `TauCeti.AInfinityAlgebra.differential_transfer` and `TauCeti.AInfinityAlgebra.mul_transfer` — the transferred $m_1$ is $d_H$ and $m_2$ is $p\, m_2 (i \otimes i)$.
- `TauCeti.AInfinityAlgebra.m_three_transfer` — the transferred $m_3$ is the three-term tree sum with its sign.
- `TauCeti.HeisenbergDGA.minimalModel_m_three` — for $\Lambda(a,b,c)$ with $dc = ab$, the roadmap's example, $m_3([a],[a],[b]) = [ac]$, nonzero by `TauCeti.HeisenbergDGA.minimalModel_m_three_ne_zero`. This fixes the sign convention: the other sign would give $-[ac]$.

## Lean subtleties
- `InternalGrading R H` is a decomposition of $H$ into pieces indexed by $\mathbb{Z}$; `LinearMap.IsHomogeneous f P Q n` says $f$ sends piece $k$ of $P$ into piece $k + n$ of $Q$.
- The side conditions of a special contraction are hypotheses: an ordinary deformation retract must first be normalised.
- The definition is `noncomputable`: $(1 + \delta K)^{-1}$ is an inverse in the endomorphism ring, which exists because $\delta K$ raises word length.
- The Koszul twist `GH.koszulTwist 1` in the third term of $m_3$ is the sign $(-1)^{|x|}$ of moving the degree $-1$ map $h$ past the first input.

## What it says
`TauCeti.AcyclicModels.IsAcyclicOn G M ε` says that a functor $G$ from a category $\mathcal{C}$ to chain complexes of $k$-modules is **acyclic on the models** $M_n$: on each model its augmented complex is exact.

- `{C} [Category C]`, `{k} [Ring k]`: a category and a ring of coefficients, not necessarily commutative.
- `(G : C ⥤ ChainComplex (ModuleCat k) ℕ)`: a functor to chain complexes of $k$-modules indexed by $\mathbb{N}$.
- `(M : ℕ → C)`: a model $M_n$ for each degree, as in a model presentation of another functor.
- `(ε : ∀ X, (G.obj X).X 0 →ₗ[k] k)`: an augmentation $G_0(X) \to k$ for every object $X$.
- Its two fields, for every $n$: `exists_d_eq_of_d_eq_zero`, every cycle of positive degree $q + 1$ in $G(M_n)$ is a boundary, so $H_q(G(M_n)) = 0$ for $q \ge 1$; and `exists_d_eq_of_augment_eq_zero`, every $0$-chain of $G(M_n)$ of augmentation $0$ is a boundary.

This is the acyclicity hypothesis of the method of acyclic models of Eilenberg and Mac Lane: the reduced homology of $G$ vanishes on each model. It is asked only on the models $M_n$, which is all the method uses, and nothing is asked of $\varepsilon$ beyond this: that it kills boundaries or is natural are separate hypotheses of the theorems that need them.

- `TauCeti.isAcyclicOn_normalizedCubicalChainComplex` — normalized cubical chains are acyclic on contractible models.

These are the instances the method is used for: on cubes and simplices both chain functors satisfy the two fields, and the comparison of cubical and singular homology follows.

## Lean subtleties
- `ChainComplex (ModuleCat k) ℕ` has $d : X_{n+1} \to X_n$; the first field quantifies over `q + 1`, so degree $0$ is covered by the second field only.
- `(G.obj X).X 0 →ₗ[k] k` is a $k$-linear map; for noncommutative $k$, of left modules.
- The structure is a `Prop`: it records existence of boundaries and chooses none.
- `M : ℕ → C` is a sequence: the same object may serve in several degrees.

## What it says
`TauCeti.AcyclicModels.ModelPresentation.homotopy` is the uniqueness half of the method of acyclic models: two natural chain maps $f, g : F \Rightarrow G$ that agree after augmentation in degree $0$ are naturally chain homotopic, when $F$ is free on models and $G$ is acyclic on those models.

- `{C} [Category C]`, `{k} [Ring k]`, `{F G : C ⥤ ChainComplex (ModuleCat k) ℕ}`: two functors to chain complexes of $k$-modules.
- `(B : ModelPresentation F)`: $F$ is free on models: in each degree $n$ a model $M_n$ and a generator $u_n \in F_n(M_n)$ such that every $x \in F_n(X)$ is $\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\, F(\sigma)(u_n)$ over $\sigma : M_n \to X$, with coefficients linear and natural in $x$, not necessarily unique.
- `{εG}`, `(hG : IsAcyclicOn G B.model εG)`: an augmentation of $G$ for which $G$ is acyclic on the models of $B$.
- `(f g : F ⟶ G)`: natural chain maps; `(hfg)`: $\varepsilon_G(f_X x) = \varepsilon_G(g_X x)$ for every $X$ and $x \in F_0(X)$.
- `(X : C)`. Its value: a chain homotopy `Homotopy (f.app X) (g.app X)`, Mathlib's structure of maps $h_{i,j} : F_i(X) \to G_j(X)$ with $f - g = dh + hd$. Naturality in $X$ is the theorem `TauCeti.AcyclicModels.ModelPresentation.homotopy_hom_naturality`; the components vanish unless $j = i + 1$.

This is the theorem of Eilenberg and Mac Lane as in Massey, with one model per degree and "agree on $H_0$" expressed through augmentations. It is the single-index case of `TauCeti.AcyclicModels.MultiModelPresentation.homotopy`, which allows a family of models in each degree.

The target lists no Checks.

With `TauCeti.AcyclicModels.ModelPresentation.chainMap` for existence, these give the natural homotopy equivalence of cubical and singular chains.

- The result is data, a specific `Homotopy`, built by choice of boundaries supplied by `hG` in a `noncomputable section`. The mathematics asserts only existence; no canonical homotopy is claimed.
- `F ⟶ G` is a morphism of functors: a natural transformation whose components are chain maps.
- Mathlib's `Homotopy` carries maps `hom i j` for all pairs $(i, j)$; here the off-shape components are $0$.

## What it says
The **Leibniz rule for the cup product of cochains** along a diagonal: for cochains $\varphi$ of degree $p$ and $\psi$ of degree $q$, $\delta(\varphi \smile \psi) = \delta\varphi \smile \psi + (-1)^p\, \varphi \smile \delta\psi$.

- `[Preadditive C] [MonoidalCategory C] [MonoidalPreadditive C] [Linear k C] [MonoidalLinear k C]`: a $k$-linear additive monoidal category with bilinear tensor product, `k` a commutative semiring.
- `{A B E : ChainComplex C ℕ} [A.HasTensor B]`: chain complexes indexed by $\mathbb{N}$, with $(A \otimes B)_n = \bigoplus_{i+j=n} A_i \otimes B_j$ existing, carrying the Koszul-signed differential.
- `(D : E ⟶ tensorObj A B)`: a chain map, the diagonal; `(μ : M ⊗ N ⟶ P)`: a pairing of coefficients.
- `(p q n : ℕ) (h : p + q = n)`, `(φ : A.X p ⟶ M)`, `(ψ : B.X q ⟶ N)`: cochains, as morphisms out of the chain objects.
- The conclusion: `E.d (n+1) n ≫ cupCochain k D μ p q n h φ ψ` equals `cupCochain … (A.d (p+1) p ≫ φ) ψ + ((-1)^p) • cupCochain … φ (B.d (q+1) q ≫ ψ)`. Here $\varphi \smile \psi : E_n \to P$ is $D_n$ followed by $\varphi \otimes \psi$ on the summand $A_p \otimes B_q$ and by $\mu$, and the coboundary of a cochain is precomposition with $d$.

This is Hatcher's Lemma 3.6 in his convention $\delta\varphi = \varphi \circ \partial$, stated for any diagonal in a monoidal category instead of the Alexander–Whitney map on singular chains, and for any pairing of coefficients. The singular cup product is the special case, and the lemma is what makes the cup product descend to cohomology.

## References and tests
- A. Hatcher, *Algebraic Topology*, Section 3.2, Lemma 3.6.
- Roadmap: [Algebraic topology, Stage 6.2, item 2 "Use Alexander–Whitney to define cup products…"](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/929496d4221b974c60787257a3cdc28b600fc49c/TauCetiRoadmap/AlgebraicTopology/README.md#L1056), which asks for "the actual cochain rule d(a∪b)=da∪b+(−1)^p a∪db for degree-p a". The target lists no Checks.

The site lists no tests of this lemma. It rests on `TauCeti.ChainComplex.d_comp_tensorCochain`, the same rule for the tensor product of cochains on $A \otimes B$, and on `D` being a chain map; `TauCeti.ChainComplex.cupCycles` and `TauCeti.ChainComplex.cup` use it to pass to cocycles and cohomology.

## Lean subtleties
- `(-1 : ℤ) ^ p • _` is the integer action on the abelian group of morphisms: the sign depends on the degree of the first cochain only.
- Coboundaries carry no sign: `A.d (p + 1) p ≫ φ` is $\varphi \circ \partial$. Conventions that put $(-1)^{p+1}$ into $\delta$ change the rule's appearance, not its content.
- `[A.HasTensor B]` is a typeclass hypothesis that the direct sums defining $A \otimes B$ exist; in a module category it holds automatically.
- Degrees are natural numbers: the rule is stated for $d : E_{n+1} \to E_n$, so nothing is said below degree $0$.
